extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, patent prosecutors, patent litigators, patent examiners, and parties in IPRs
extracted.subtask_description: Legal standard and evidentiary framework for determining whether an inventor’s prior acts (sales, uses, publications) constitute a ‘‘publicly disclosed’’ disclosure that excludes a later-filed patent application from being prior art under 35 U.S.C. § 102(b)(2)(B) (AIA). Focus is on whether the subject matter was made available to the public before the other filing’s effective date.

rubrics_metrics.name: § 102(b)(2)(B) 'publicly disclosed' requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutory text: a disclosure shall not be prior art under subsection (a)(2) if 'the subject matter disclosed had, before such subject matter was effectively filed under subsection (a)(2), been publicly disclosed by the inventor.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To qualify for the (b)(2)(B) exception, the inventor must have 'publicly disclosed' the subject matter before the effective filing date of the other patent application. The court treats this phrase as a material statutory requirement distinct from the broader term 'disclosed' used elsewhere in §102. The exception is limited to subject matter the inventor made available to the public; mere private acts that are not public do not satisfy this requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between 'disclosed' and 'publicly disclosed' (statutory-language reading)
rubrics_metrics.description: The opinion emphasizes that the statute uses different phrases—'disclosed' versus 'publicly disclosed'—and that the added word 'publicly' suggests a narrower meaning than the generic term 'disclosed.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not equate every 'disclosure' in §102(a) with being 'publicly disclosed' for purposes of §102(b)(2)(B). Because Congress used different wording, 'publicly disclosed' must be interpreted to carry the additional requirement of public availability; treating the terms as identical would render the word 'publicly' superfluous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose-based standard: 'made available to the public' test
rubrics_metrics.description: The statutory exception is intended to protect inventors who disclosed their invention to the public prior to another’s later-filed application. The Court reads 'publicly disclosed' to mean it is reasonable to conclude the invention was made available to the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret 'publicly disclosed' with the statute’s purpose in mind: the patent bargain rewards bringing new technology into the public domain. Thus, assess whether the subject matter was made available to the public (not merely commercially exploited or privately sold). If the public has not actually learned the relevant aspects of the invention, the exception should not apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private sale (non-confidential) does not necessarily 'publicly disclose'
rubrics_metrics.description: A private (non-confidential) sale to a single purchaser arranged via private communications does not automatically constitute a 'publicly disclosed' disclosure under §102(b)(2)(B).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A finding that a device was sold privately—e.g., arranged by private messages, sale to a single purchaser, no publicity, no evidence of wider distribution or fulfillment—will typically be insufficient to show the inventor 'publicly disclosed' the subject matter. Anti-pattern: relying only on testimony of a private sale without evidence the subject matter was made accessible to the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public use vs. public disclosure distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court distinguishes 'public use' (relevant to §102(a)(1)) from 'publicly disclosed' under §102(b)(2)(B): a public commercial use can be invalidating prior art without having 'publicly disclosed' all inventive features to the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conflate commercial exploitation/public use (which can create an invalidating bar) with the separate concept of making the invention available to the public for purposes of the §102(b)(2)(B) exception. A use or sale may be 'public' in the sense of commercial exploitation yet still not have made the inventive subject matter publicly accessible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Helsinn precedent: sale is a 'disclosure' under §102(a)(1) but not necessarily 'publicly disclosed' under §102(b)(2)(B)
rubrics_metrics.description: The opinion recognizes Helsinn (Supreme Court) that a private commercial sale can constitute a 'disclosure' under §102(a)(1), but stresses that that ruling does not resolve whether such a sale 'publicly disclosed' the invention for §102(b)(2)(B).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When arguing §102(b)(2)(B), acknowledge Helsinn's holding about 'disclosure' but distinguish it: showing a sale exists is not enough; you must separately show the sale resulted in public availability of the subject matter. Helsinn supports that sales can be disclosures, but the (b)(2)(B) exception requires public dissemination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative history / printed-publication accessibility analogy
rubrics_metrics.description: The floor debate indicates that 'whether an invention has been made available to the public is the same inquiry that is undertaken under existing law to determine whether a document has become publicly accessible.' The opinion cites legislative statements and the Cordis decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In uncertain cases, apply tests analogous to printed-publication/public-accessibility doctrine (e.g., was the information sufficiently publicly accessible?) when assessing whether the inventor 'publicly disclosed' the subject matter. Example: distribution to a limited number of entities without legal obligation of confidentiality might still fail to be 'publicly accessible' (Cordis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary showing required to prove public disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent owner seeking the §102(b)(2)(B) exclusion must show that the inventor publicly disclosed the subject matter before the other filing’s effective date; mere proof of a private sale is inadequate without evidence of publicization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical proof elements that support 'publicly disclosed' include public advertising, publications, broad distribution, fulfillment and public availability of products, or other indicia that the inventive features were open to public inspection/knowledge. Anti-patterns: relying solely on private communications, private courier delivery to a single buyer, unfulfilled large orders, or unverifiable statements that do not show public accessibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of related §102(b) exceptions: (b)(1)(A)/(b)(2)(A) vs (b)(1)(B)/(b)(2)(B)
rubrics_metrics.description: §102(b)(1)(A) and (b)(2)(A) provide exceptions for disclosures 'made by the inventor or . . . by another who obtained the subject matter disclosed directly or indirectly from the inventor' (and do not include a 'publicly disclosed' requirement). By contrast, subsections (b)(1)(B) and (b)(2)(B) concern disclosures by another after the inventor 'publicly disclosed' the subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate which statutory exception is invoked. If relying on (b)(1)(A) or (b)(2)(A), proof of direct/indirect derivation from the inventor is controlling and publicness is not required. If relying on (b)(1)(B) or (b)(2)(B), you must demonstrate the inventor made a public disclosure before the third party’s disclosure or filing.
